questions.question: What are the most important Spring annotations every developer should know?
questions.title: Essential Spring Annotations Overview
questions.direct_answer: Important Spring annotations are easiest to learn by job: bean definitions (@Configuration, @Bean), component roles (@Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller), injection (@Autowired, @Qualifier, @Value), web mappings (@RestController, @GetMapping), transactions (@Transactional), and lifecycle callbacks (@PostConstruct, @PreDestroy). Each annotation is processed only when the relevant Spring infrastructure manages the class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth of Spring annotation knowledge across configuration, dependency injection, and lifecycle management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Knowing web annotations but not configuration or lifecycle annotations, or treating all stereotypes as identical
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Organize annotations by category and explain the purpose of each group with concrete use cases

sections.title: Spring Annotations by Responsibility
sections.content:
Annotations are metadata, not executable magic on any object. new PaymentService() is not processed merely because the class contains @Value or @Transactional. The class must be a Spring bean and the relevant post-processors/configuration must be active.

Use specialized stereotypes where they express real intent, but do not assume every stereotype adds behavior by itself. Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies. Put validation on boundary DTOs, transactions around complete use cases, and lifecycle cleanup only on resources the bean truly owns.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Configuration annotations define or import bean metadata.
Stereotypes make classes candidates for component scanning and communicate their role.
Injection annotations resolve dependencies/configuration for managed objects.
Web, transaction, validation, and lifecycle annotations need their corresponding infrastructure.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @Configuration and @Bean explicitly define objects. @Service and @Repository identify application and persistence components discovered by scanning. A class with one constructor normally needs no @Autowired; @Qualifier or @Primary resolves multiple candidates. @RestController and @GetMapping declare an MVC HTTP handler. @Transactional is commonly applied through a proxy, and @PostConstruct runs after dependency population. The useful answer explains the category and boundary rather than reciting one long list.

sections.title: Core Spring Annotations
sections.content:
amber|Stereotypes|~Register beans|@Component / @Service|@Repository / @Controller|Scanned automatically
blue|Wiring|~Inject deps|@Autowired|@Qualifier / @Primary|@Value for props
emerald|Configuration|~Define beans|@Configuration / @Bean|@ComponentScan|@SpringBootApplication
violet|Web and Data|~Build features|@RestController / @RequestMapping|@Transactional|@Profile

sections.title: Practical Annotation Usage Across Categories
Without: Field Injection (Harder to Test)
With: Constructor Injection (Preferred)
When to Use Each Annotation Category
sections.content:
Use **configuration annotations** (@Configuration, @Bean) when you need explicit control over bean creation — third-party library classes, conditional beans, or complex initialization logic.

Use **stereotype annotations** (@Service, @Repository, @Component) for your own application classes to let Spring auto-detect and manage them.

Use **injection annotations** (@Autowired, @Qualifier, @Value) to wire dependencies and inject external configuration.

Use **web annotations** (@RestController, @GetMapping, @PostMapping) to build REST APIs and map HTTP requests to methods.

Use **lifecycle annotations** (@PostConstruct, @PreDestroy) when you need initialization logic after dependency injection or cleanup before shutdown — like opening database connections, starting background threads, or releasing resources.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Component for everything**: Freshers often use @Component for all classes instead of specific stereotypes like @Service or @Repository. This works but loses semantic meaning — @Repository adds persistence exception translation, @Service marks business logic, and @Controller handles web requests. Use the right stereotype for clarity and framework benefits.
- **Forgetting @ComponentScan scope**: Annotations only work if Spring scans the package. If your @Service is in com.example.external but your main class is in com.example.app, Spring won't find it. Always ensure components are in the same package or subpackages as your @SpringBootApplication class.
- **Mixing field and constructor injection**: Using @Autowired on fields is tempting but makes testing harder. Constructor injection (implicit @Autowired on the only constructor) is preferred — it makes dependencies explicit and enables immutability with final fields.

seo.metaTitle: Essential Spring Annotations Overview — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What are the most important Spring annotations every developer should know? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: One annotation barely scratches the surface. Interviewers want to see how the annotation families fit together.
speakable_v2.standard_example: OrderService (@Service), OrderRepository (@Repository), and OrderController (@RestController) in a Spring Boot app

beats.text: Spring annotations fall into five families. Configuration defines beans. Stereotypes mark a class as a bean, and @Component is the catch-all stereotype. Injection wires dependencies. Web maps HTTP calls. Lifecycle hooks run setup and cleanup. Knowing the families beats a flat list.
Spring used to wire everything through XML. That got verbose fast. Annotations move the same wiring next to your code, so it's easier to read. Each family replaces one chunk of the old XML setup.

items: Configuration: @Configuration and @Bean define beans by hand. Handy for third-party classes.
Stereotypes: @Service, @Repository, and @Controller register your own classes. Spring scans them all the same way.
Injection: @Autowired, @Qualifier, and @Value wire dependencies and config values.
Lifecycle: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy run right after wiring and just before shutdown.

beats.text: Picture an OrderService marked @Service. It uses constructor injection to pull in an OrderRepository marked @Repository. An OrderController marked @RestController handles the web side. Here's the non-obvious part. @Repository also maps database errors to Spring exceptions. So the right stereotype does more than label a class.

items: Don't slap @Component on everything. The right stereotype shows intent. It also unlocks framework perks.
Don't forget the lifecycle pair. Learners skip @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy, and interviewers love asking about them.

speakable_v2.cap: Group them by family from configuration to lifecycle. That shows architecture sense, not annotation trivia.

questions.question: What is @Value annotation in Spring?
questions.title: @Value Annotation in Spring Explained
questions.direct_answer: @Value can inject an individual property placeholder such as ${server.port}, a default such as ${timeout:30}, or a Spring Expression Language expression such as #{2 * 5} into a Spring-managed bean. Use it for a small number of isolated settings. Use @ConfigurationProperties for a related group that benefits from type-safe binding and validation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Property injection knowledge and understanding of externalized configuration in Spring
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the difference between ${} for property placeholders and #{} for SpEL expressions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between ${} for property values and #{} for SpEL expressions with concrete examples

sections.title: Using @Value for an Individual Setting
sections.content:
Property placeholders and SpEL are different. ${...} asks the Environment for configuration; #{...} evaluates an expression. They can be nested, but complicated expressions in annotations become hard to test and maintain.

Constructor parameters make injected configuration visible and testable. Never print secrets, even partially, in teaching examples. If a property should be validated as a group or documented for IDE completion, @ConfigurationProperties plus validation and metadata is the clearer model.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: ${name} resolves a property from Spring's Environment.
${name:default} supplies fallback text when the key is absent.
#{expression} evaluates SpEL; use it only when expression power is actually needed.
@Value is not processed on objects created directly with new outside Spring.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A constructor can accept @Value("${payment.timeout:5s}") Duration timeout. Spring resolves the winning property source and converts the text to Duration when conversion support is available. A missing required placeholder normally fails context creation, which is useful for required configuration. Do not hide a required secret behind an unsafe default. For base URL, timeout, retry count, and credentials together, bind PaymentProperties instead.

sections.title: @Value at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Inject external values|From properties or env|Into fields or params|Config, not hardcoded
blue|Syntax|~Two forms|${property.key} for properties|#{SpEL} for expressions|Default with ${key:default}
emerald|Where to Use|~Fields or constructor|@Value on a parameter|Prefer constructor|Type converted automatically
rose|Watch Out|~Missing property|Fails at startup|Unless a default is given|Prefer @ConfigurationProperties for groups

sections.title: Property and SpEL Injection Examples
Without: Hardcoded Configuration
With: Externalized via @Value
When to Use @Value
sections.content:
Use @Value when you need to inject **simple configuration values** that change between environments — API keys, URLs, timeouts, feature flags, or numeric thresholds. It's perfect for values in application.properties that differ in dev versus prod.

Use **property placeholders ${key}** for straightforward value injection.

Use **SpEL expressions #{expression}** when you need to compute values at startup, like calculating a derived rate or concatenating strings.

Use **default values ${key:default}** to make your app resilient when properties are missing, especially for optional features.

Avoid @Value for complex configuration — if you have ten related properties, use **@ConfigurationProperties** instead, which binds a whole group of properties to a Java object. Don't use @Value in classes you instantiate with new — it only works on Spring-managed beans created by the container.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing ${} and #{}**: Freshers often mix up dollar-brace for property placeholders and hash-brace for SpEL. ${server.port} reads a property, #{2 + 2} evaluates an expression. Using ${2 + 2} won't compute anything, it'll look for a property literally named "2 + 2".
- **Forgetting defaults for optional properties**: If you use @Value("${optional.feature}") without a default and the property is missing, the app crashes at startup. Always provide defaults with colon: ${optional.feature:false}.
- **Using @Value on non-Spring beans**: If you create a class with new PaymentService(), @Value does nothing. Spring must create the bean for injection to work.
- **Hardcoding values instead of externalizing**: Freshers sometimes use @Value("localhost") instead of @Value("${database.host}"). The whole point is to read from properties files so you can change config without recompiling.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @Value with ${} and #{}?
How do you inject a list from application.properties?
When should you use @ConfigurationProperties instead of @Value?

seo.metaTitle: @Value Annotation in Spring Explained — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is @Value annotation in Spring? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: @Value is the one annotation that drops a config value straight into a field. No hardcoding required.
speakable_v2.standard_example: @Value("${server.port}") and ${key:default} in a Spring Boot service

beats.text: @Value reads a value from the Spring Environment and injects it into a field or constructor parameter. ${server.port} pulls a property. `#{...}` syntax runs a SpEL expression. Add a colon for a fallback, like ${timeout:30}.

Hardcoded config makes every change a redeploy. @Value pushes those values out to application.properties or environment variables. You tweak one file, and every bean that reads it picks up the change.

items: ${key} reads a property as text. Spring converts it to int, boolean, or a List for you.
${key:default} uses the fallback when the key is missing, so startup won't crash.
#{expression} evaluates SpEL, so it can do math or call a bean method.
For a whole cluster of related settings, @ConfigurationProperties beats a pile of @Value lines.

beats.text: Say PaymentService needs an API key and a timeout. The constructor takes @Value("${payment.api.key}") and @Value("${payment.timeout:5000}"). The timeout defaults to 5000 when nobody sets it. Here's the non-obvious part. @Value only fires on Spring-managed beans, so a new PaymentService() gets nothing.

items: Mixing up the braces. Dollar-brace reads a property, `#{...}` syntax runs an expression.
Skipping the default on optional keys. A missing key with no fallback crashes startup.

speakable_v2.cap: @Value is great for one-off settings. For a group of related properties, reach for @ConfigurationProperties instead.
followup_handoff: What happens at startup when a @Value key is missing and has no default?

questions.question: What is @Profile in Spring and when do you use it?
questions.title: @Profile Annotation in Spring Explained
questions.direct_answer: @Profile makes a component or @Bean definition active only when a profile expression matches the Environment's active profiles. @Profile("dev") enables it for dev; @Profile("!prod") matches when prod is not active. Profiles select bean/configuration variants at context creation. Profile-specific config files change values and are related, but they are not the same mechanism.

interviewer_intent.testing: Profile-based configuration knowledge and environment-specific bean creation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing @Profile on beans with profile-specific properties files like application-dev.properties
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example of different DataSource implementations per profile and explain profile activation methods

sections.title: Activating Beans with @Profile
sections.content:
Profile expressions support !, &, and | under Spring's profile expression rules. The default profile is used only when no explicit profile is active. Avoid setting spring.profiles.active from a profile-specific document where activation rules can become invalid/confusing; let the deployment select active profiles.

Test missing and multi-profile combinations. If dev and prod variants both become active and implement one interface, injection can become ambiguous unless the design prevents it.

**Example.** A LocalMailConfig annotated @Profile("dev") can register a console mail sender, while ProdMailConfig with @Profile("prod") registers the real provider. Setting spring.profiles.active=dev activates only the development choice.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Place @Profile on a component, configuration class, or @Bean method.
Activate profiles through deployment configuration, command-line options, tests, or other Environment sources.
Several profiles can be active together; design combinations so required beans are not ambiguous.
Do not use profiles as a substitute for runtime feature flags that must change without restart.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A LocalMailConfig can provide a logging MailSender under @Profile("dev"), while a production integration is active under @Profile("prod"). In many cases it is simpler to keep one auto-configured DataSource and change only URL/credentials through application-dev.properties and application-prod.properties rather than hand-writing profile DataSource beans. Profiles decide which definitions exist; config data supplies their values.

sections.title: @Profile at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Conditional beans|Active only in a profile|dev / test / prod|Env-specific wiring
blue|How to Activate|~Set the active profile|spring.profiles.active|Env var or arg|Multiple allowed
emerald|When to Use|~Per-environment beans|Mock vs real services|Different DataSources|Feature toggles
violet|Pairs With|~Related tools|@Configuration classes|@ActiveProfiles in tests|@Conditional underneath

sections.title: Profile-Specific DataSource Configuration
When to Use @Profile
sections.content:
Use @Profile when you need **fundamentally different bean implementations** across environments. Classic use case: different databases per environment (H2 for dev, PostgreSQL for prod).

Use it for **mock versus real external services** — a stub payment gateway in dev, the real Stripe integration in prod.

Use it for **performance versus debugging trade-offs** — verbose logging in dev, optimized logging in prod.

Use it when **local development needs differ from cloud deployment** — local file storage versus AWS S3. Activate profiles via command-line: --spring.profiles.active=dev, environment variable SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod, or in application.properties. You can activate multiple profiles simultaneously: dev,debug means both dev and debug beans are created. Don't use @Profile for simple property changes — use profile-specific properties files like application-dev.properties instead. Reserve @Profile for when the bean class itself must differ.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing @Profile with profile-specific properties**: Freshers think @Profile("dev") and application-dev.properties are the same. They're complementary. Profile-specific properties change configuration values. @Profile changes which beans exist. Use properties for values, @Profile for implementations.
- **No default profile**: If you mark all DataSource beans with @Profile and forget to activate a profile, Spring has no DataSource and the app crashes. Always provide a @Profile("default") bean or use @Profile("!prod") to mean "anything except prod".
- **Hardcoding profile checks**: Freshers write if (activeProfile.equals("dev")) instead of using @Profile. This scatters environment logic everywhere. Let Spring handle it declaratively.
- **Not testing profile activation**: In production, you set spring.profiles.active=prod via environment variable or command-line. Freshers forget to test this and deploy without activating the right profile, causing the app to use the wrong database.

followup_questions: How do you combine multiple profiles?

seo.metaTitle: @Profile Annotation in Spring Explained — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is @Profile in Spring and when do you use it? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: @Profile is a switch on a bean. It only flips on when the matching environment is active.

beats.text: @Profile makes a bean exist only when a named profile is active. Mark a bean or a @Configuration class with @Profile("dev") and it shows up only under the dev profile. You turn a profile on with spring.profiles.active.
Dev, test, and prod need different wiring. You don't want an in-memory H2 database in prod, or a live payment gateway in dev. @Profile picks the right bean per environment without any if-statements.

items: @Profile("dev") creates the bean only when dev runs.
@Profile("!prod") creates it everywhere except prod.
@Profile({"dev", "test"}) covers dev or test together.
On a @Configuration class, every @Bean inside follows that profile.

beats.text: Picture DevConfig as @Configuration @Profile("dev") building an H2 datasource. ProdConfig is @Profile("prod") building a MySQL one. Run with dev and H2 wins. Deploy with prod and MySQL wins. Here's the non-obvious part. OrderService never knows. It just @Autowires DataSource.

items: Don't confuse @Profile with application-dev.properties. One picks beans, the other picks values.
If no bean matches the active profile, an @Autowired injection blows up at startup.

speakable_v2.cap: @Profile is your environment gate. One annotation flips which bean exists, with zero conditional code in your services.
followup_handoff: How do @Profile and application-dev.properties work together?
What happens when a required bean only exists in an inactive profile?

questions.question: What is @Conditional in Spring and how does it work?
questions.title: @Conditional Annotation in Spring
questions.direct_answer: @Conditional registers a configuration class or @Bean only when its Condition matches while the context is being built. Spring Boot provides focused conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, and @ConditionalOnProperty. These are startup/configuration-time decisions for the ApplicationContext, not live per-request checks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of conditional bean registration and how Spring Boot auto-configuration decides which beans to create
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @Conditional runs at every bean lookup instead of once at application startup during context initialization
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how @ConditionalOnClass checks for library presence on classpath and mention that this is how Spring Boot detects if you have H2 or MongoDB and auto-configures the right data source

sections.title: Conditional Bean Registration
sections.content:
Conditions are central to Boot auto-configuration because defaults must back off when dependencies or user beans are absent/present. Ordering matters: a missing-bean condition sees the definitions available when evaluated, which is why auto-configuration ordering is controlled.

For application code, prefer clear property/profile conditions over one large custom Condition. Use ApplicationContextRunner tests to cover match and no-match cases for reusable auto-configuration.

**Example.** A custom Condition can register UnixFileWatcher only when the operating system and a required path match. In Boot, focused conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnProperty cover common classpath and configuration cases.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: A Condition reads metadata and context/environment facts before bean creation.
Use Boot's built-in conditions for classpath, bean, property, resource, and web-application checks.
Use @Profile when the condition is naturally an active-profile expression.
Custom conditions should be deterministic and avoid instantiating application beans during evaluation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: An optional cache configuration can use @ConditionalOnClass for the cache library and @ConditionalOnMissingBean for the application override. A property switch can use @ConditionalOnProperty with an explicit havingValue. If the condition does not match, its bean definition is not registered. Changing the property after startup normally does not add the bean; rebuild/refresh behavior requires separate infrastructure.

sections.title: @Conditional at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Register a bean only if|A Condition matches|A runtime check|Flexible bean creation
blue|How It Works|~Implement Condition|matches() returns boolean|Evaluated at startup|Controls registration
emerald|Boot Variants|~Ready-made|@ConditionalOnProperty|@ConditionalOnClass / Missing|Powers auto-config
violet|When to Use|~Env-driven wiring|Optional features|Library defaults|Toggle by config

sections.title: Custom @Conditional with Multiple Built-in Variants
When to Use @Conditional
sections.content:
Use @Conditional when you need **environment-specific beans** like separate CacheManager implementations for dev (simple in-memory) versus production (Redis).

Use it for **optional feature integration** — if you have an optional Kafka dependency, create KafkaTemplate bean only when kafka-clients JAR is present using @ConditionalOnClass.

Use it for **graceful degradation** — create a FullTextSearchService bean when Elasticsearch is available, but fall back to DatabaseSearchService when it's not using @ConditionalOnMissingClass.

Use it in **library development** when building Spring Boot starters to auto-configure beans only when users have the right dependencies. For example, if you're building a monitoring starter, create MetricsCollector bean only when Micrometer is on the classpath.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Condition Evaluation Timing**: Freshers think @Conditional checks happen every time you @Autowire the bean. Actually, the condition runs once during application startup when Spring builds the context. If matches returns false, the bean is never created at all.
- **Public Condition Classes**: Writing the Condition implementation as a private inner class fails because Spring can't instantiate it. Always make your Condition class public and ensure it has a no-arg constructor.
- **Overusing Custom Conditions**: Creating complex custom Condition classes when Spring Boot already provides @ConditionalOnProperty or @ConditionalOnBean. Check the 20+ built-in @Conditional variants before writing your own — @ConditionalOnWebApplication, @ConditionalOnExpression, @ConditionalOnResource all solve common cases.

followup_questions: How would you write a custom @Conditional condition?

seo.metaTitle: @Conditional Annotation in Spring — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is @Conditional in Spring and how does it work? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: @Conditional is the engine under Spring Boot's auto-configuration. It decides whether a bean gets built at all.

beats.text: @Conditional gates a bean behind a runtime check. You give it a class that implements Condition, and its matches method returns true or false. True builds the bean. Spring Boot ships dozens of ready-made variants on top of it.

Spring Boot's auto-config stays out of your way on purpose. It builds a default bean only when you haven't built your own. @ConditionalOnMissingBean is the trick. Register your bean and Boot's version backs off.

items: @ConditionalOnClass builds a bean when a class sits on the classpath.
@ConditionalOnMissingBean builds it only when no such bean exists yet.
@ConditionalOnProperty builds it when a property holds a given value.
Custom check: implement Condition and return true or false from matches.

beats.text: Say you want a beta feature toggle. The bean carries @ConditionalOnProperty with beta.feature.enabled and havingValue true. In dev the property is true, so the bean exists. In prod it's absent, so the feature stays off. Here's the non-obvious part. The check runs once at startup, not on every call.

items: Don't use @Conditional where @Profile already fits. Profiles handle environment, @Conditional handles logic.
Stacked conditions must all pass. For OR logic, write one custom Condition class.

speakable_v2.cap: @Conditional keeps Spring Boot non-invasive. Learn @ConditionalOnMissingBean and @ConditionalOnProperty, and auto-config stops feeling like magic.
followup_handoff: How do you override an auto-configured bean with @ConditionalOnMissingBean?
How would you write a custom Condition class?

questions.question: What is @Transactional in Spring and what does it do?
questions.title: @Transactional in Spring Explained
questions.direct_answer: @Transactional declares a transaction boundary that Spring usually applies through a proxy. The transaction manager starts or joins a transaction before an intercepted method and commits when it completes normally. By default, RuntimeException and Error trigger rollback; checked exceptions do not unless rollback rules are configured. A call from one method to another on the same object normally bypasses proxy interception.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of declarative transaction management and how Spring proxies enforce transactional boundaries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @Transactional only works on public methods called from outside the class because Spring uses proxy-based AOP
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the rollback behavior: by default rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error) but not on checked exceptions, and mention you can customize this with rollbackFor attribute

sections.title: What @Transactional Actually Controls
Quick revision
content: Transaction behavior is applied by a configured PlatformTransactionManager.
Proxy interception means external calls through the Spring bean are the normal boundary.
Default rollback: RuntimeException and Error; configure rollbackFor for checked exceptions when needed.
Database transactions make supported resource changes atomic, not arbitrary external side effects such as email or HTTP calls.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @Transactional removes manual begin, commit, and rollback code around a unit of database work. In the common proxy mode, the caller must invoke the Spring-managed proxy. The interceptor asks the chosen transaction manager to create or join a transaction, calls the method, and then commits or rolls back according to the result and rollback rules. A self-invocation such as this.saveInsideTransaction() does not cross the proxy, so the inner annotation is normally not applied. The default rollback rule covers unchecked exceptions and Error, not every Throwable.

sections.title: @Transactional at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Wraps a method in a tx|Commit on success|Rollback on a runtime ex|An atomic unit of work
blue|How It Works|~An AOP proxy|Begins/commits around the call|Same proxy is same tx|Self-calls bypass it
emerald|Key Settings|~Tune behavior|propagation|isolation|readOnly / rollbackFor
rose|Watch Out|~Common traps|No rollback on checked ex|Self-invocation skips the proxy|Must be a public method

sections.title: Service Layer with Transaction Management
Without: Self-Invocation Defeats @Transactional
With: Cross-Bean Call Goes Through the Proxy
When to Use @Transactional
sections.content:
Use @Transactional on **service layer methods** that perform multiple database operations that must succeed or fail together, like creating an order and updating inventory.

Use it for **write operations** where data consistency is critical — user registration that creates a User record and sends a welcome email record must be atomic.

Use **readOnly = true** for query methods to optimize performance, as it allows the database to skip locking and change tracking.

Use **rollbackFor** parameter when you need to roll back on checked exceptions — by default, Spring only rolls back on RuntimeException, but payment processing might throw checked PaymentException that should trigger rollback.

Apply it at the **class level** on service classes when most methods need transactions, then use @Transactional(propagation = NOT_SUPPORTED) on specific read-only methods that don't need transactional behavior.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Self-Invocation Problem**: Calling a @Transactional method from another method in the same class doesn't start a transaction because you're bypassing the Spring proxy. If methodA calls methodB in the same service, and methodB is @Transactional, no transaction is created. The solution is to inject the service into itself or refactor to call across beans.
- **Private Method Annotation**: Putting @Transactional on private or protected methods does nothing because Spring uses JDK or CGLIB proxies that only intercept public methods. Spring won't even warn you — the annotation is silently ignored.
- **Checked Exception Rollback**: Freshers assume all exceptions trigger rollback, but by default only unchecked exceptions do. If you throw IOException or your custom checked exception, the transaction commits anyway unless you add rollbackFor = Exception.class. This causes data inconsistency bugs that are hard to debug.

followup_questions: Why doesn't @Transactional work on private methods?
What is the self-invocation problem with @Transactional?
What is transaction propagation in Spring?

seo.metaTitle: @Transactional in Spring Explained — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is @Transactional in Spring and what does it do? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: @Transactional wraps your method in a database transaction. Success commits, a runtime error rolls everything back.
speakable_v2.standard_example: OrderService.placeOrder with @Transactional rolling back on InsufficientStockException

beats.text: @Transactional runs a method inside a database transaction. Spring wraps the bean in a proxy. The proxy opens a transaction. It calls your method. It commits on success. A runtime exception triggers a rollback. Checked exceptions don't roll back unless you add rollbackFor.

Without it you'd hand-write beginTransaction, commit, and rollback around every data call. That boilerplate clutters your logic. @Transactional moves it into the framework through AOP. Your method just does business work.

items: Default rollback covers RuntimeException and Error. Checked exceptions commit anyway.
rollbackFor=Exception.class extends rollback to checked exceptions too.
readOnly=true hints a read-only transaction and speeds up reads.
Public methods only. The proxy can't intercept private or self-called methods.

beats.text: OrderService.placeOrder is @Transactional. It saves the order and reduces inventory in one transaction. If the reduce throws InsufficientStockException, Spring rolls both back. The order never saves. Here's the non-obvious part. Calling placeOrder from another method in the same class skips the proxy. No transaction starts.

items: Don't put @Transactional on private methods. The proxy ignores them with no warning.
Don't call a @Transactional method from the same class. That self-call skips the proxy, so move it to another bean.

speakable_v2.cap: @Transactional handles transactions for you. Remember the rollback rules, the public-method limit, and the self-invocation trap.
followup_handoff: What is transaction propagation, and how do REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW differ?
How does the self-invocation problem relate to Spring's AOP proxy?
